name: Rosewood
lede: Rosewood is a dark brownish red, named for the wood of the rosewood tree.

sections.title: The color of a timber
sections.body:
Paterson defines the French *bois de rose* as the dark, rich brown color of rosewood [1]. His dictionary's color index files rosewood among the reds, not the browns, which shows how the word floats between the two [2]. Our own records first list it in the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 [3]. The swatch here is a deep red-brown, darker and redder than a lot of polished rosewood.

The name is the wood's, and the wood's dark red-brown grain is the sample.

sections.title: A dyer's rosewood
sections.body: A sixteenth- or seventeenth-century recipe, as the Pigment Compendium quotes it, tells the maker to pulverise gum lac and soak it in a lye of rosewood or vinewood to draw out its color [4]. Here the rosewood supplies an alkaline solution, not a color of its own, but it shows the word was in use in the workshop by then.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive the swatch appears in 411 paintings, as photographed, more common than 71% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1400s at 3.5 times the baseline rate, and in 62% of 203 paintings it plays an accent [3]. It travels with reddish brick and black-brown [3]. Similar names include [[mahogany]], [[maroon]] and [[chestnut]].
